explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. The text says Amaziah "…did what was right in the eyes of the LORD…" (2 Kings 14:3). Amaziah, the new king of Judah, gets a good mark here. Hold onto that, because the very next words add a catch.

Not quite, friend. The text says Amaziah "…did what was right in the eyes of the LORD…" (2 Kings 14:3). So the verse tells us he does what is right in the LORD's eyes. There's a catch coming in the same verse, but that first part is a good one.

That's it, baker. The text says Amaziah "…did everything as his father Joash had done." (2 Kings 14:3). Joash was the king before him. Amaziah is following Dad's example instead of King David's, and I can tell you it's easy to just keep doing what you watched somebody else do.

No uncle in this verse, friend. The text says Amaziah "…did everything as his father Joash had done." (2 Kings 14:3). Joash was the king before him. If an uncle had been in the kitchen, the Bible doesn't say so.

No brother in this verse, friend. The text says Amaziah "…did everything as his father Joash had done." (2 Kings 14:3). Joash was the king who came before him. So the pattern he follows comes from his dad, not a sibling.

Right on the money, baker. The text says "…the people continued sacrificing and burning incense on the high places." (2 Kings 14:4). The high places were not taken away, so the people just kept right on doing it. Same habit, same spots.

Not that one, friend. The text says "…the people continued sacrificing and burning incense on the high places." (2 Kings 14:4). Nothing about drills or marching. It's a worship habit that never got cleared out.

I wish, friend, but no. The text says "…the people continued sacrificing and burning incense on the high places." (2 Kings 14:4). Nothing there about reading the Law. The high places were not taken away, and the old habit stayed with them.

Not this time, friend. The text says "…Amaziah executed the servants who had murdered his father the king." (2 Kings 14:5). No pardon is mentioned. Once the kingdom was firmly in his grasp, he dealt with them.

No banishing here, friend. The text says "…Amaziah executed the servants who had murdered his father the king." (2 Kings 14:5). It happened as soon as the kingdom was firmly in his grasp. Sending them away isn't in the story.
Careful, friend, this one's the opposite. The text says "…he did not put the sons of the murderers to death…" (2 Kings 14:6). He went by the Book of the Law of Moses instead. The sons were spared.

You've got it, baker. The text says "…he did not put the sons of the murderers to death…" (2 Kings 14:6). He acted according to what is written in the Book of the Law of Moses. Each person answers for their own sin, and that's the rule he followed.
Yes, baker. The command says, "Fathers must not be put to death for their children…" (2 Kings 14:6). A father isn't put to death for what his kids did. That's the first half of the rule.

Good one, baker. The command says, "…children must not be put to death for their fathers…" (2 Kings 14:6). A child isn't put to death for what a father did. That's the second half, and it's the command Amaziah follows when he doesn't put the murderers' sons to death.

Neighbors don't show up in this command, friend. It says, "Fathers must not be put to death for their children, and children must not be put to death for their fathers…" (2 Kings 14:6). It's all family, parent and child. Each is to die for his own sin.

Servants aren't in this command, friend. It says, "Fathers must not be put to death for their children, and children must not be put to death for their fathers…" (2 Kings 14:6). The servants did the murder, but the rule here is about parents and children.

Masters aren't in this command, friend. It says, "Fathers must not be put to death for their children, and children must not be put to death for their fathers…" (2 Kings 14:6). The rule stays inside the family, and each is to die for his own sin.

That's the number, baker. "Amaziah struck down 10,000 Edomites in the Valley of Salt." (2 Kings 14:7). That's a heavy part of the story, and the text gives the number plainly. He also took Sela in battle and called it Joktheel.
Too low, friend. The text says "Amaziah struck down 10,000 Edomites in the Valley of Salt." (2 Kings 14:7). That's ten times your number. The Edomites took a real beating.
Way too low, friend. The text says "Amaziah struck down 10,000 Edomites in the Valley of Salt." (2 Kings 14:7). That's a whole lot more than five hundred. It was a big win for Judah.
True, baker. Amaziah "…took Sela in battle and called it Joktheel, which is its name to this very day." (2 Kings 14:7). New city, new name. And the new name stuck.

Other way around, friend. Amaziah "…took Sela in battle and called it Joktheel, which is its name to this very day." (2 Kings 14:7). So Sela got a brand new name. The writer even says it was still the name when the book was written.

explanations.answer: Come and meet me face to face
explanations.explanation: That's the message, baker. Amaziah sent messengers to Jehoash, who was king of Israel, and said, "Come, let us meet face to face…" (2 Kings 14:8). That's a bold thing to say. The text doesn't tell us why he said it.

explanations.answer: Send me gold for my temple
explanations.explanation: No gold request in this message, friend. Amaziah's words were, "Come, let us meet face to face…" (2 Kings 14:8). It sounds like a challenge to me, but that's my guess. The text only gives us those words.

Not this one, friend. The Edomites were already beaten by then (2 Kings 14:7). Amaziah's message to Jehoash, king of Israel, was, "Come, let us meet face to face…" (2 Kings 14:8). No team-up offer in there.

explanations.answer: The cedar's daughter for its son
explanations.explanation: Right, baker. The thistle says, "Give your daughter to my son in marriage." (2 Kings 14:9). A little thistle asking a big cedar for that? Boy, that's some nerve.

explanations.answer: A place in the cedar's shade
explanations.explanation: Not shade, friend. The thistle's message was, "Give your daughter to my son in marriage." (2 Kings 14:9). It's a marriage request. That's a lot bigger than asking for a cool spot.
No seeds in this story, friend. The thistle's message was, "Give your daughter to my son in marriage." (2 Kings 14:9). It wanted a marriage between the families. That's a much bigger ask than seeds.
That's the ending, baker. "…a wild beast in Lebanon came along and trampled the thistle." (2 Kings 14:9). Poor little thistle. It asked for a lot and got flattened.

No wind in this story, friend. The text says, "…a wild beast in Lebanon came along and trampled the thistle." (2 Kings 14:9). Something with feet did the job. The thistle had asked for a cedar's daughter, and a beast came along.

No woodcutter here, friend. The text says, "…a wild beast in Lebanon came along and trampled the thistle." (2 Kings 14:9). It's a beast, and it trampled. The thistle is the one that sent the message asking for a marriage.
That's the word, baker. Jehoash says, "You have indeed defeated Edom, and your heart has become proud." (2 Kings 14:10). Those are his words about Amaziah. He's saying the win went to Amaziah's head.
Not afraid, friend. Jehoash says, "You have indeed defeated Edom, and your heart has become proud." (2 Kings 14:10). Proud is the word he picks. Those are his words about Amaziah.

Not weary, friend. Jehoash says, "You have indeed defeated Edom, and your heart has become proud." (2 Kings 14:10). Those are his words, and proud is the one he chose. Weary doesn't show up in what he says.

explanations.answer: Enjoy the win and stay home
explanations.explanation: Yep, baker. Jehoash says, "Glory in that and stay at home." (2 Kings 14:10). In other words, you won, so take a bow and stay put. I'd call that free advice.
The opposite, friend. Jehoash says, "Glory in that and stay at home." (2 Kings 14:10). He's telling Amaziah to stay put, not march north. No army trip invited.
No gift here, friend. Jehoash says, "Glory in that and stay at home." (2 Kings 14:10). He tells Amaziah to glory in his win and stay home. Nothing in the text about sending anything.

True, baker. Jehoash asks, "Why should you stir up trouble so that you fall—you and Judah with you?" (2 Kings 14:10). He's saying Amaziah's fall wouldn't be just his own. Judah would go down with him.

It's in there, friend. Jehoash asks, "Why should you stir up trouble so that you fall—you and Judah with you?" (2 Kings 14:10). He warns Amaziah that Judah could fall too. That's the heart of his warning.
Not so, friend. The text says "…Amaziah would not listen…" (2 Kings 14:11). He didn't stay home. He heard the warning and didn't take it.
Right, baker. The text says "…Amaziah would not listen…" (2 Kings 14:11). He didn't stay home. Jehoash advanced, and the two kings ended up facing each other.

explanations.answer: Judah is routed and runs home
explanations.explanation: That's how it went, baker. "…Judah was routed before Israel, and every man fled to his home." (2 Kings 14:12). That's a rough day. Every man headed home.
Not a win, friend. The text says "…Judah was routed before Israel, and every man fled to his home." (2 Kings 14:12). Routed means beaten badly. It wasn't close.

explanations.answer: The battle ends in a truce
explanations.explanation: No truce here, friend. The text says "…Judah was routed before Israel, and every man fled to his home." (2 Kings 14:12). Judah lost and the men ran for home. A truce isn't in the story.
That's right, baker. "…Jehoash king of Israel captured Amaziah king of Judah…" (2 Kings 14:13). It happened right there at Beth-shemesh. The king who asked for a meeting got caught.
Not this time, friend. The text says "…Jehoash king of Israel captured Amaziah king of Judah…" (2 Kings 14:13). Amaziah didn't make it away. Jehoash is the one who went on to Jerusalem.

Amaziah lived through this one, friend. The text says "…Jehoash king of Israel captured Amaziah king of Judah…" (2 Kings 14:13). He was captured, not killed. The text also says he lived fifteen years after the death of Jehoash (2 Kings 14:17).

explanations.answer: The house of the LORD and the palace
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Jehoash took "…all the gold and silver and all the articles found in the house of the LORD and in the treasuries of the royal palace…" (2 Kings 14:14). Both places are named. That was a heavy loss for Judah.

explanations.answer: The houses of the city's elders
explanations.explanation: Not the elders' houses, friend. The text says Jehoash took the gold and silver "…found in the house of the LORD and in the treasuries of the royal palace…" (2 Kings 14:14). Those two places are named. Elders' houses aren't mentioned.

explanations.answer: The storerooms by the city gates
explanations.explanation: Not the storerooms, friend. The text says Jehoash took the gold and silver "…found in the house of the LORD and in the treasuries of the royal palace…" (2 Kings 14:14). Those are the two places named. The gates come up in the verse before, where Jehoash breaks down the wall from the Ephraim Gate to the Corner Gate (2 Kings 14:13).

True, baker. Jehoash took "…some hostages. Then he returned to Samaria." (2 Kings 14:14). The hostages came along with the gold and silver. Then he headed back to Samaria, where he was later buried (2 Kings 14:16).
Not false, friend. The text says Jehoash took "…some hostages. Then he returned to Samaria." (2 Kings 14:14). He took people along with the gold and silver. Then he headed home.

True, baker. The verse says it plainly: "Amaziah son of Joash king of Judah lived for fifteen years after the death of Jehoash son of Jehoahaz king of Israel." (2 Kings 14:17). Jehoash is the king of Israel who beat him at Beth-shemesh. Amaziah was still around fifteen years after Jehoash was gone.

Other way around, friend. "Amaziah son of Joash king of Judah lived for fifteen years after the death of Jehoash son of Jehoahaz king of Israel." (2 Kings 14:17). Jehoash died first. Amaziah kept going for fifteen more years.

That's the place, baker. The text says Amaziah "…fled to Lachish." (2 Kings 14:19). He ran when the conspirators plotted against him in Jerusalem. Running didn't solve it, because men were sent after him to Lachish, and they killed him there.
Not Hebron, friend. The text says Amaziah "…fled to Lachish." (2 Kings 14:19). That's the city he ran to. Hebron isn't in this passage.
Not Jericho, friend. The text says Amaziah "…fled to Lachish." (2 Kings 14:19). That's where he ran. Jericho isn't in this part of the story.
Sadly not, friend. The text says "…men were sent after him to Lachish, and they killed him there." (2 Kings 14:19). He wasn't safe. I think this part of the story is a heavy one.
That's right, baker. The text says "…men were sent after him to Lachish, and they killed him there." (2 Kings 14:19). Running to Lachish didn't keep him safe. It's a heavy part of the story.

That's him, baker. "…all the people of Judah took Azariah, who was sixteen years old, and made him king in place of his father Amaziah." (2 Kings 14:21). Sixteen years old and handed a kingdom. I think that's a lot to carry.

Close, friend, but not that one. Jeroboam was Jehoash's son and took over in Israel (2 Kings 14:16). In Judah, "…all the people of Judah took Azariah…" and made him king (2 Kings 14:21). Two kingdoms, two new kings.

Not Jotham, friend. The text says "…all the people of Judah took Azariah, who was sixteen years old, and made him king in place of his father Amaziah." (2 Kings 14:21). Azariah is the name in this passage. Jotham doesn't come up here.
